prompt:
Use case: illustration-story.
Create a square watercolor storyboard, ideally 1536×1536, exactly TWO columns by THREE rows, six independent 3:2 LANDSCAPE panels in row-major order. Equal cells with a narrow clear ivory paper gap, no borders, labels or frames; no scene crosses a cell boundary. Keep the full primary subject inside the central 82% of each cell.
MEDIUM ONLY is shared: sophisticated adult editorial watercolor on warm ivory cold-pressed paper, transparent layered washes, expressive pencil contours, irregular pigment edges softly dissolving into unpainted paper. Sage, terracotta, lavender, soft ochre with scene-appropriate blues and greens. Loose believable anatomy and gestures, not photographic, not 3D, not cartoon. Warm and adult, but do NOT impose golden sunshine or a cozy room on every setting.
Each panel illustrates the SPECIFIC QUESTION supplied, not merely the topic. Make the action or idea readable without a caption. Change the subject, action, setting, scale or viewpoint substantially for every panel. A close crop of a prop from the preceding scene is not a new concept. Use the concrete directions below, no decorative filler or invented extra scenes.
Fictional adults and natural hands/gestures are welcome where specified; use candid back/side/over-shoulder views or crop naturally above the chin, never blank faceless heads. No idealized romance, no default gender roles, no recognizable real person. Adults of ordinary appearance, varied skin tones. These are fictional examples, not reconstructions of a user's memories. Emotion can be mixed; do not visually assert reconciliation or a promised outcome.
STRICTLY NO cups, mugs, drinking glasses, plates, cutlery, kettles, table settings, flower vases, decorative bouquets, hearts, rings, floating icons, puzzle metaphors, UI, captions, letters, numbers, handwriting, logos or watermarks. No café, Tuscan room or wicker furniture unless expressly requested. Book pages, maps, tickets and screens must have no readable writing. Do not fill unrelated panels with the same furniture, fabric or object.
Cast this fictional pair as two ordinary women in their fifties, one with short silver hair, the other with dark curls. No idealized fashion or romance poses.
STORY S02: That is so us
PANEL 1
Question context (do not render as text): What is one moment with me that still makes you laugh?
Recognition cue: Shared laughter
Paint: Two fictional adults on a windswept walk burst into a shared laugh as their small umbrella turns inside out. A candid full-body scene, ordinary rain jackets, harmless mishap, wind and body language make the laugh visible.
PANEL 2
Question context (do not render as text): What was going on just before that funny moment?
Recognition cue: Before the funny moment
Paint: Wide scene just before the mishap: the same two adults step out of a shelter, one opens the umbrella carefully while the other struggles playfully with a flapping jacket hood. The setup, not the punchline.
PANEL 3
Question context (do not render as text): What part of that moment makes you laugh the most?
Recognition cue: The funniest detail
Paint: Close lively detail of the umbrella now inside out above a bewildered adult's crooked rain hood; the other adult's amused side profile enters the edge. Focus on the one ridiculous visual detail, no exaggerated cartoon anatomy.
PANEL 4
Question context (do not render as text): What makes that joke feel like one of ours?
Recognition cue: Our private joke
Paint: After the gust has passed, the adults exchange a knowing sideways look and both copy the same tiny crooked-hood gesture with their own jackets. A shared private reference shown through mirrored behavior, different viewpoint and scale.
PANEL 5
Question context (do not render as text): How would you tell that funny story to someone who was not there?
Recognition cue: Retelling the story
Paint: One adult animatedly retells the umbrella story to a third adult who was not there, arms showing the umbrella's unexpected flip; their partner smiles beside them holding the now-folded umbrella. Clear storytelling scene in an ordinary hallway.
PANEL 6
Question context (do not render as text): If you like, give our funny story a name to keep.
Recognition cue: A name for the joke
Paint: A little unlettered illustrated keepsake tag attached to the folded umbrella, bearing only a tiny hand-painted inside-out umbrella silhouette; a specific funny memory given a recognizable visual name, no words or tableware.
